disease_info: Binge-Eating Disorder is characterized by recurrent episodes of consuming unusually large amounts of food in a discrete period, accompanied by a sense of loss of control, and followed by marked distress or guilt. Unlike bulimia nervosa, it is not regularly associated with inappropriate compensatory behaviors such as purging, fasting, or excessive exercise. The course is often chronic or relapsing, with onset frequently linked to stress, negative affect, or longstanding issues around weight and body image, and it can occur across a wide range of body sizes. It commonly co-occurs with mood and anxiety disorders and may fluctuate in severity with life stressors, interpersonal difficulties, or health-related concerns.

narrative.personality: Marissa is a meticulous, tech-curious tradeswoman who channels her constant worry into safety, precision, and a quietly competitive drive to master new systems while nurturing a reflective artistic side.
narrative.stressor: About six months ago, Marissa’s long-standing joint pain and shortness of breath worsened, and her primary care doctor warned her that she was bordering on needing surgery and stricter work restrictions if she did not address her weight and blood pressure. Already prone to worry, she reacted by trying to impose rigid rules on herself—skipping meals on long service days, delaying lunch to finish jobs, and then coming home exhausted and famished after evening call-outs. Over several months, this pattern of pushing through physically demanding shifts, ignoring her own needs, and then using food late at night to quickly unwind and "make up" for missed meals became entrenched, leaving her feeling ashamed and increasingly secretive about how she was eating at home and on the road between jobs. She finally sought psychiatric care after realizing that her attempts to control her eating through stricter dieting were backfiring, and that her eating patterns were starting to undermine both her energy on the job and her confidence to manage her health risks.
narrative.chief_complaint: I’ve started eating my meals so fast that I barely taste them, and I feel like I can’t slow myself down once I start.

narrative.personality: Claudette is an organized, community-minded cleaner with a nurturing, artistic streak, who takes pride in creating harmonious spaces while occasionally acting on impulsive urges in small, comforting ways.
narrative.stressor: Following a difficult divorce last year, Claudette’s evenings shifted from noisy family dinners to coming home alone after late custodial shifts, with her adult children living in other cities and her ex-partner cutting off contact. At first she filled the quiet with church volunteering and extra hours at the community center, but conflict with her ex over finances and custody of shared possessions, along with seeing him quickly move on to a new relationship, left her feeling rejected and deeply self-conscious about her appearance and aging. She began bringing home takeout or large amounts of comfort foods after work and eating them in her small kitchen late at night, telling herself it was her "reward" for a hard day but feeling embarrassed by how much she was consuming and avoiding eating around church friends or at theater potlucks. Over roughly five months, these private eating episodes became her primary way to cope with loneliness and hurt, and she finally came to psychiatric treatment after a church mentor gently confronted her about withdrawing from social meals and she admitted feeling out of control and ashamed about her secret eating.
narrative.chief_complaint: I’ve started avoiding meals with other people because I’m embarrassed by how much I end up eating when I’m by myself.

narrative.personality: Aleta is a sharp, socially engaged retired educator with a competitive, highly organized streak, who delights in learning and community projects while occasionally overextending herself and overlooking her own basic needs.
narrative.stressor: After her husband’s death three years ago, Aleta slowly rebuilt a full life through choir, book clubs, and leading an intergenerational literacy project, priding herself on staying as active as she was in her working years. However, over the past year several close friends moved away or became less mobile, and her own mild mobility and medication issues made her give up driving at night, forcing her to cut back on evening social activities and shared meals. In response, she poured even more energy into daytime commitments and meticulous budgeting for her programs, often skipping or delaying meals while out and then eating quickly and alone when she finally got home, treating food as an afterthought until she realized she was routinely finishing entire portions before noticing she was full. Over about five months this hurried, solitary eating pattern became a source of distress and self-criticism, and she sought psychiatric help after her daughter expressed concern that Aleta seemed preoccupied with her eating habits and was "rushing through" meals in a way that didn’t match her otherwise careful, deliberate nature.
narrative.chief_complaint: Lately I find myself eating my meals much faster than I intend to, almost like I’m racing through them without meaning to.
